subject: languages
title: Memory Management & Garbage Collection
summary: How languages decide where values live and when they die: stack and heap, manual memory and its bugs, reference counting, tracing and generational collectors, modern low-pause GCs in Java and Go, and Rust's ownership and borrowing.

lessons.title: Storage and object lifetimes
lessons.summary: A conventional call stack reclaims frames in last-in, first-out order; language storage durations and optimisations are more general
lessons.body:
Programs need storage for materialised values, and finite storage eventually needs to be reused. Optimisation can remove a value entirely; long-lived storage can remain until process exit. Two common storage mechanisms are the **call stack** and **heap memory**, usually just called "the stack" and "the heap". Registers, static storage and optimizations also matter; this is an introductory model, not a complete classification.

The difference is about **object lifetime**: how long a value stays valid. A conventional call frame is reclaimed on return, while block-scoped object lifetimes can end earlier. Heap allocations can outlive the allocating call; reclamation follows ownership, reachability or explicit deallocation rather than actual future need. The rest of this module is really about the heap, so it pays to understand why the stack is the easy case.

> [!note] Scope of this module
> The Operating Systems subject covers virtual memory, pages and how `malloc` carves up memory internally. Here we take the language-level view: who decides when a value dies, and how.

## The call stack

In a conventional stack implementation, an active call has a **stack frame** for saved state and locals that need memory. Parameters and the return address may instead be held in registers, and optimisation can remove frames. Returning reclaims that frame; individual language-level object lifetimes can end earlier.

```
 main() calls area(), which calls sq()

 high addresses
 +----------------------+
 | main:  w=3, h=4      |
 +----------------------+
 | area:  a=3, b=4      |
 |        ret -> main   |
 +----------------------+
 | sq:    n=3           |  <- stack pointer
 |        ret -> area   |
 +----------------------+
 low addresses (grows down on x86/ARM)
```

A conventional fixed-size frame can have a fast path that moves the **stack pointer** register by a fixed amount, sometimes in one instruction. Freeing it is moving the pointer back. The simple LIFO fast path needs no free-list search. Function prologues, stack alignment, stack checks, page faults and runtime stack growth can add work; cache residency is not guaranteed.

The catch is that the stack is strictly **last in, first out**. A conventional frame belongs to its active call. Many frames have a statically known size, though C variable-length arrays and other dynamic stack allocations are counterexamples.

## The heap

The **heap** is a large pool of memory where blocks can be allocated and freed in any order. Heap storage is commonly useful when:

1. A value must **outlive the function** that created it (returning a new object, storing it in a global or a long-lived data structure).
2. The **size is only known at run time** (reading a file of unknown length, a list that grows).
3. The value is **large** (a 50 MB image would blow the stack).
4. The value is **shared** between threads or parts of the program with unrelated lifetimes.

Heap allocation often costs more, although bump-pointer heap allocators also have cheap fast paths: the allocator must find a free block, record its size and later reclaim it. The really hard question is **when to free it**, because its lifetime need not coincide with the allocating call. That question is the subject of every other lesson in this module.

## Trade-offs at a glance

| | Stack | Heap |
|---|---|---|
| Allocate | move a pointer | allocator call |
| Free | automatic, at return | manual or GC |
| Lifetime | active frame | allocation contract |
| Size | bounded; often fixed | allocator limits |

Performance-minded code in managed languages tries to **avoid heap allocation in hot loops**: reuse allocations, prefer values over pointers in Go, and let escape analysis keep short-lived objects off the heap. Every avoided allocation is also work the garbage collector never has to do.

## Key takeaways
- A conventional call stack reclaims frames in last-in, first-out order; language storage durations and optimisations are more general.
- Heap storage permits lifetimes independent of a call, but dynamic size, sharing and large size alone do not logically require it.
- Allocation fast paths are implementation choices; stack checks, allocator bookkeeping and reclamation add work.

questions.prompt: Why can a conventional fixed-size stack-frame allocation have a cheap fast path?

options.text: The stack lives in faster RAM chips than the heap
options.explanation: Both commonly use the same virtual-memory and RAM system. Different placement, caching and faults can affect speed; the cheap LIFO allocation mechanism does not require faster RAM chips.

options.text: Allocating a frame is just moving the stack pointer by a fixed amount, and freeing it is moving it back
options.explanation: Correct. LIFO placement allows a stack-pointer adjustment rather than a free-list search. Prologues, checks, alignment, faults and growth can add work; heap bump allocation can also be cheap.

options.text: The operating system pre-zeroes stack memory, so no work is needed
options.explanation: Zero-filled newly mapped pages do not eliminate frame setup, checks or bookkeeping. C automatic locals without initialisers are not generally initialised by the language.

options.text: Stack values are never freed, so there is no deallocation cost
options.explanation: A conventional call frame is reclaimed on return. Individual object lifetimes can end earlier, and optimized values need not occupy physical frame slots.

questions.workedExample:
For an illustrative downward-growing fixed-size stack, a frame uses the next contiguous region below the current stack pointer. Returning restores the previous pointer. A heap allocator can also have a bump-allocation fast path, so this compares mechanisms rather than guaranteeing a speed ranking.

```formula
sp_after = sp_before − F
sp_after = 10,000 − 64 = 9,936
sp_back = sp_after + F
sp_back = 9,936 + 64 = 10,000
where
sp_before: the illustrative byte address in the stack-pointer register before allocation, 10,000 here
sp_after: its byte address after allocating the frame
F: the fixed frame size, 64 bytes here
sp_back: the restored byte address after return
In words: this fixed-size downward-growing stack allocates by subtraction and restores by addition, without searching a free list.
```

The fast path can resemble `sp -= frame_size` and `sp += frame_size`. Prologues, alignment, checks, page faults and stack growth add work. Storage in the expired frame cannot retain a live object after return.

questions.prompt: Which value most clearly calls for storage surviving the allocating call, commonly a heap allocation?

options.text: A loop counter `i` used inside one function
options.explanation: A counter whose lifetime is one call is the textbook stack value: fixed size and dies when the function returns.

options.text: A fixed-size `int point[2]` used only inside the function that declares it
options.explanation: Small, fixed-size and confined to one call: the stack handles this perfectly.

options.text: A list of lines read from a file of unknown length, returned to the caller
options.explanation: Correct. Its size is only known at run time and it must outlive the function that builds it. Both are reasons for the heap.

options.text: A function parameter `n` of type `int`
options.explanation: Parameters live in the callee's frame (or registers) and die with the call. No heap needed.

questions.workedExample:
Ask the four heap questions for each value:

| Value | Outlives call? | Size at run time? |
|---|---|---|
| loop counter | no | no |
| `point[2]` | no | no |
| file lines | **yes** | **yes** |
| parameter `n` | no | no |

Only the list of lines fails the stack's rules: it must survive the return, and the compiler cannot know how big a frame it would need.

This is a common design choice, not a proof that dynamic size or sharing always requires the heap. Caller-provided storage, static storage and other lifetime arrangements can be alternatives.

lessons.title: Automatic lifetimes and Python references
lessons.summary: A pointer to an expired C automatic object cannot safely be dereferenced, regardless of the output in a quick experiment
lessons.body:
A returned pointer must still designate a live object. C makes the programmer obey storage-duration rules; Python names instead refer to managed objects. The same assignment spelling can therefore have very different consequences.

## The classic bug: returning a stack address

C distinguishes storage durations; it does not require a physical stack. Automatic locals commonly use frames or registers, static locals use static storage, and malloc obtains allocated storage.

```c
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Return does not extend x's lifetime. */
int *bad(void) {
    int x = 42;
    return &x;   /* frame dies here */
}

int *good(void) {
    int *p = malloc(sizeof *p);
    /* Allocation failure transfers
     * nothing. */
    if (!p) return NULL;
    *p = 42;
    return p;    /* caller must free */
}
```

`bad` returns a pointer to an automatic object whose lifetime has ended; a conventional stack frame is only the implementation model. Accessing the expired object is undefined behaviour regardless of whether later calls reuse that storage; no particular output or crash is guaranteed. Clang warns: *address of stack memory associated with local variable 'x' returned*. `good` returns NULL on allocation failure; on success the caller has a new duty: call `free(p)` once and only once.

## Python: names reference managed objects

CPython represents values as objects with type and reference-management metadata. Most are dynamically allocated; some singleton/static objects and immortal objects are exceptions, and free-threaded builds have different counting details. Some objects, such as `None` and cached small integers, are shared rather than freshly allocated for each use; exact creation and caching details belong to the CPython implementation. A local variable is just a name in the frame that **refers** to an object.

```python
# The returned reference keeps the list
# alive.
def make():
    xs = [1, 2, 3]   # list object on heap
    return xs        # return the reference

a = make()       # list survives the call
```

The list survives this call because `a` still refers to it. That is why "stack vs heap" rarely comes up in Python: you never place anything yourself, and the runtime manages reclamation; cycles and finalization complicate promptness.

## Value and reference semantics

Placement is tied to what assignment means:

- **Value semantics**: assignment copies the data. C structs, Go structs and arrays, and Rust's `Copy` types behave this way.
- **Reference semantics**: assignment copies a pointer, so two names share one object. Python objects and Java objects behave this way.

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = a          # same list, not a copy
# Mutate the shared list through b.
b.append(3)
print(a)       # [1, 2, 3]
```

The list cannot be reclaimed while either name still strongly retains it. Other aliases can retain it too, so reclamation must account for every strong path, not only these two names.

## Key takeaways
- A pointer to an expired C automatic object cannot safely be dereferenced, regardless of the output in a quick experiment.
- CPython names refer to managed objects; retaining the returned list keeps that list alive.
- Assigning a Python list to another name shares the list rather than copying it.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = a
# append changes the selected list.
b.append(3)
print(a)
```

options.explanation: This assumes `b = a` copies the list (value semantics). In Python, assignment copies only the reference, so both names point at one heap object.
Correct. There is one list object on the heap and two names referring to it. Appending through `b` changes the object that `a` also sees.
Only one `append` runs, on one object. Nothing appends twice.

options.text: An error, because `a` and `b` cannot share a list
options.explanation: Sharing objects through multiple references is normal in Python; it is what reference semantics means.

questions.workedExample:
1. `a = [1, 2]` creates a list object on the heap and binds the name `a` to it.
2. `b = a` binds `b` to the **same** object. No copy is made.

```
a --+
    +--> [1, 2]
b --+
```

3. `b.append(3)` mutates that object to `[1, 2, 3]`.
4. `print(a)` follows `a` to the same object: `[1, 2, 3]`.

To get an independent copy you would write `b = a.copy()` or `b = list(a)`.

options.text: `x` is a global variable, so other threads overwrite it
options.explanation: `x` is a local (automatic) variable, not a global. The problem is its lifetime, not sharing between threads.

options.text: `printf` cannot print through a pointer
options.explanation: Dereferencing a valid `int *` with `*p` is fine. The pointer is the problem, not `printf`.

options.text: x has automatic storage duration ending at return; accessing it afterward is undefined behavior
options.explanation: Correct. Stack reuse is one possible manifestation, not a necessary condition or guaranteed explanation of observed output.

options.text: The compiler automatically moves `x` to the heap, but frees it before `printf`
options.explanation: Go permits such a returned pointer by preserving the value's lifetime. C requires its own storage-duration rules to be obeyed; optimization cannot make access to this expired automatic object defined.

questions.workedExample: The lifetime of x ends when get returns. Reading through the returned pointer is undefined behavior immediately; optimization or later frame reuse can produce arbitrary symptoms, and no particular value or crash is guaranteed. Return an int value, use caller-provided storage, or allocate and check heap storage with documented ownership.

lessons.title: Placement and escape analysis
lessons.summary: HotSpot escape analysis can eliminate an object allocation through scalar replacement; it does not promise to put every non-escaping object on a stack
lessons.body:
The language model describes observable behaviour; a compiler may use registers, inline fields or eliminate allocations while preserving it. This table is a starting model, not a physical-layout guarantee.

## How each language places values

| Language | Stack | Heap |
|---|---|---|
| C | many automatic locals; placement optimized | allocated storage from malloc |
| CPython | interpreter frames (details vary by version) | most objects; some shared or static objects |
| Java | local slots conceptually; may be registers | objects in JVM model; allocations may be eliminated |
| Go | non-escaping values | escaping values |
| Rust | local values often inline or registers | owned allocations through Box, Vec, String |



## Java: frame values and semantic heap objects

The JVM model gives methods local-variable slots and places class instances and arrays in the heap. Machine-code placement can differ: HotSpot can keep locals in registers or eliminate an allocation while preserving observable behaviour.

```java
void f() {
    int n = 10;            // in frame
    // JVM model: a refers to a new array.
    int[] a = new int[n];  // ref in frame,
                           // array on heap
}
```

The HotSpot JIT compiler performs **escape analysis**: if it can prove an object never leaves the method, it may eliminate the allocation entirely and keep the fields in registers ("scalar replacement"). You cannot request this; it is an optimisation.

## Go: the compiler decides with escape analysis

Go makes escape analysis visible. You can return a pointer to a local variable, and it is perfectly safe:

```go
type Point struct{ X, Y int }

func newPoint() *Point {
    p := Point{1, 2}
    // The pointed-to value must survive.
    return &p   // fine in Go
}
```

Analyzed as a non-inlined function returning an escaping pointer, p requires storage surviving the call and the standard compiler normally heap-allocates it. Inlining can change the result at a particular call site. Use go build -gcflags=-m to inspect decisions; nonescaping values can still need heap storage for implementation reasons such as size.

Things that commonly force a value to escape in Go: returning its address, storing it in a global or a heap object, capturing it in a closure that outlives the call, or storing an interface value in an escaping location. Merely forming a pointer or interface does not universally force heap allocation.

## Key takeaways
- HotSpot escape analysis can eliminate an object allocation through scalar replacement; it does not promise to put every non-escaping object on a stack.
- Go can safely return a pointer to a local because its storage must survive the call; inlining changes particular allocation decisions.
- A pointer or interface value alone does not universally force Go heap allocation; inspect compiler diagnostics for the actual context.

## Further reading
- [Stack-based memory allocation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack-based_memory_allocation)
- [Escape analysis — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escape_analysis)
- [A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector (escape analysis section) — go.dev](https://go.dev/doc/gc-guide)
- [Go FAQ: stack or heap? — go.dev](https://go.dev/doc/faq#stack_or_heap)
- [What is ownership? (stack and heap) — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)
- [Primary verification source 1](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [Primary verification source 2](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html)
- [Primary verification source 3](https://go.dev/src/runtime/stack.go)
- [Primary verification source 4](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/refcounting.html)

options.text: It returns a dangling pointer, exactly like the C equivalent
options.explanation: That is C's behaviour. Go's compiler tracks pointers out of a function and never lets a stack slot be referenced after the frame dies.

options.text: It fails to compile: you cannot take the address of a local
options.explanation: Taking `&p` of a local is legal and idiomatic Go.

options.text: Escape analysis sees that `p` outlives the call and allocates it on the heap; the GC frees it later
options.explanation: Correct. `go build -gcflags=-m` reports `moved to heap: p`. The pointer is valid for as long as anyone holds it.

options.text: `p` is copied into the caller's stack frame on return
options.explanation: The return type is a pointer, not a Point copy. Inlining and caller context can sometimes eliminate heap allocation, but that is excluded by this question’s premise.

questions.workedExample:
1. The compiler runs escape analysis on `newPoint`.
2. It sees `&p` flowing out through the return value.
3. A stack slot cannot survive the return, so `p` is allocated on the heap instead.
4. The returned pointer refers to that heap object, and the garbage collector reclaims it once nothing references it.

If `newPoint` returned `Point` (a value) instead, `p` could stay on the stack and be copied out, costing the GC nothing.

Assume Point is declared as struct{ X,Y int }. The language guarantees the pointer remains valid, not a fixed placement decision at every optimized call site.

questions.prompt: Analyzing these Go functions without inlining into callers, with returned references retained, which locals escape? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Escapes. The address leaves the function through the return value, so `x` must outlive the frame.

options.text:
```go
func b() int {
    x := 1
    p := &x
    return *p
}
```
options.explanation: Does not escape. `p` is used only inside `b` and only the value `*p` is returned, so `x` can stay on the stack. Taking an address does not by itself force a heap allocation.

options.text:
```go
var g *int

func c() {
    x := 1
    g = &x
}
```
options.explanation: Escapes. Storing the address in a global means it is reachable after `c` returns.
Escapes. The returned closure captures `c` by reference and outlives `d`, so `c` must live on the heap.

questions.workedExample:
The rule: a value escapes if a reference to it can be reached after its function returns.

| Fn | Reference leaves? | Escapes |
|---|---|---|
| a | via return | yes |
| b | no, only a copy | no |
| c | via global | yes |
| d | via closure | yes |

You can confirm each with `go build -gcflags=-m`, which can report escaping x in a/c and captured c in d; diagnostic wording depends on the compiler. Optimized call-site behavior can differ.

options.text: count is a primitive local value in f’s frame model
options.explanation: True. Local primitives live in the frame (or registers) and vanish when `f` returns.

options.text: a is a reference local in f’s frame model
options.explanation: True in the JVM frame model: a local slot holds a reference value. The JVM specification does not prescribe that reference's physical width or machine-code location.

options.text: The array object is allocated on the stack because `a` is a local
options.explanation: False. In Java's model every object, including arrays, is on the heap. Only the reference is local. (The JIT may optimise away a non-escaping allocation, but that is an optimisation, not the semantics.)

options.text: The array becomes eligible for garbage collection once `f` returns
options.explanation: True. After the return no reference to the array exists, so the next collection that examines it can reclaim it.

questions.workedExample:
Separate the variable from the object it refers to:

```
 frame of f        heap
 +-----------+     +--------------+
 | n         |     | int[n]       |
 | count     |     | 0 0 0 ...    |
 | a  -------+---> +--------------+
 +-----------+
```

1. `count` and `a` are locals, so both live in the frame.
2. `new` always creates the object on the heap.
3. When `f` returns, the frame and the only reference disappear, so the array is unreachable and collectable.

Optimized machine code may keep locals in registers or eliminate them and the array. The array may become unreachable before return after its last possible use.

questions.prompt: A Java developer says: "My `Point` objects are created and discarded inside one hot loop, so the JVM puts them on the stack." What is the most accurate response?

options.text: Correct: the JVM always stack-allocates objects that are created inside a loop
options.explanation: The JVM makes no such guarantee. Placement depends on the JIT's analysis of each allocation site after inlining.

options.text: Wrong: Java objects are always heap-allocated and every one costs a GC allocation
options.explanation: Too strong. Semantically objects are on the heap, but HotSpot's C2 compiler can eliminate allocations it proves never escape.

options.text: Partly right: if the JIT's escape analysis proves the object never escapes, it can scalar-replace it, keeping its fields in registers or the frame with no heap allocation
options.explanation: Correct. HotSpot C2 can scalar-replace eligible allocations. Escape and scalar-replacement eligibility depend on compiler analysis; nonescaping alone is not a guarantee.

options.text: Wrong: escape analysis is only done by Go, never by the JVM
options.explanation: HotSpot has done escape analysis since Java 6 (`-XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis`, on by default). Go simply makes its version visible with `-gcflags=-m`.

questions.workedExample: The JVM object model does not promise stack allocation. HotSpot C2 can eliminate some allocations by scalar replacement, making their fields locals or registers. Non-inlined calls or storage into escaping objects can obstruct analysis, but using a nonescaping object as a lock need not: escape analysis can also eliminate locking. Measure the optimized allocation behavior.

lessons.title: Owned buffers and stack budgets
lessons.summary: Vec and String own heap buffers through local metadata; Box has a different representation, and zero-sized or empty allocations are special cases
lessons.body:
Ownership and physical placement answer different questions. A small local handle can own a large allocation elsewhere; a stack budget must account for the storage actually materialised in frames.

## Rust: ownership and explicit allocations

Rust values can live in locals, registers, static storage or inside another allocation. Box owns a heap allocation, while Vec and String usually own a heap buffer. A local Vec or String commonly has inline pointer/length/capacity metadata; a Box<T> for sized T has a pointer-sized representation, not those three fields, and its heap buffer is freed automatically when the owner goes out of scope.

```
 let v = vec![1, 2, 3];

 stack            heap
 +----------+     +---+---+---+
 | ptr  ----+---> | 1 | 2 | 3 |
 | len  = 3 |     +---+---+---+
 | cap  = 3 |
 +----------+
```

## Stack limits and stack overflow

Conventional OS threads have their own stacks; the standard Go runtime also manages separate goroutine stacks. Stack limits and growth policies differ from the available heap.

| Runtime | Typical stack size |
|---|---|
| Linux main thread | configured limit; inspect ulimit -s |
| JVM platform thread | platform/version-dependent; configure -Xss |
| Go standard runtime goroutine | small growable stack; implementation-dependent |
| CPython | interpreter recursion limit; inspect sys.getrecursionlimit() |

Deep recursion can exhaust a stack or encounter a runtime recursion guard. A C program has no language-guaranteed stack-overflow exception; a protected stack commonly faults. Java may throw `StackOverflowError`. The standard Go runtime reports a fatal stack-limit error; debug.SetMaxStack documents an initial maximum of 1,000,000,000 bytes on 64-bit systems. Python raises `RecursionError` at its interpreter recursion limit; excessive limits can still crash a process.

Goroutine stacks are a neat trick. They start tiny and, when a function needs more room, the runtime allocates a bigger stack and copies the old one across, fixing up pointers into it. That is why a Go program can run hundreds of thousands of goroutines when the same number of 1 MB OS-thread stacks would not fit.

> [!warning] Big arrays on the stack
> If double is 8 bytes and the array is materialized on the stack, `double grid[2000][2000];` needs 32,000,000 bytes, exceeding an 8 MiB stack budget. Allocate it on the heap instead.

To check whether a local array fits, multiply its element count by the size of one element and compare the result with the thread's stack budget:

```formula
S_grid = 2000 × 2000 × 8 B
S_grid = 32,000,000 B
S_stack = 8 MiB = 8 × 1,048,576 B
S_stack = 8,388,608 B
S_grid / S_stack ≈ 3.8
where
S_grid: the memory the array needs, in bytes (B): rows × columns × bytes per element
2000: the number of rows, and also the number of columns, in grid[2000][2000]
8: the size of one C double (a 64-bit floating-point number) on common platforms, in bytes
S_stack: the thread's stack budget, in bytes; 8 MiB is a common Linux default for the main thread, but it is configurable
B: bytes; one byte is 8 bits
MiB: mebibyte, 2^20 = 1,048,576 bytes (binary prefix; a megabyte, MB, is 1,000,000 bytes)
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: the array needs about 3.8 times the whole stack budget, before counting any other frame, so it cannot fit.
```

The same multiplication works for any fixed-size local: a 100-row, 100-column grid of eight-byte doubles needs 80,000 bytes and fits within the illustrative 8 MiB budget when that much space remains. The budget is not fixed: it depends on the operating system, `ulimit -s` and how the thread was created.

> [!note] Limits of this model
> A universal stack size or allocation latency is omitted: neither is guaranteed across runtimes, operating systems and compiler settings. Dynamic size and sharing alone do not require heap storage (C VLAs and safely scoped sharing are counterexamples).

## Key takeaways
- Vec and String own heap buffers through local metadata; Box has a different representation, and zero-sized or empty allocations are special cases.
- Thread and goroutine stack budgets depend on runtime, platform and configuration; recursion limits are not interchangeable with byte limits.
- Compare a materialised array's byte requirement with the whole available stack budget, including existing frames and other overhead.

S_stack = 8 MiB = 8 × 1,048,576 B
S_stack = 8,388,608 B
N = S_stack / S_frame

where
S_stack: the thread's stack budget, in bytes (B)
MiB: mebibyte, 2^20 = 1,048,576 bytes (binary prefix)

N: the number of frames (nested calls) that fit

questions.prompt: For a materialized local Vec<i32> on a conventional target with 8-byte pointers and usize, use the standard pointer/length/capacity model. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The Vec value has pointer, length and capacity metadata: 24 bytes in this model
options.explanation: The default-allocator Vec guarantees this triplet; field order is not promised and optimized locals need not occupy physical stack slots.

options.text: The three `i32` elements (12 bytes) live in a heap buffer owned by `v`
options.explanation: True. `vec!` allocates a heap buffer and the `Vec` owns it.

options.text: The vector's heap buffer is freed when the garbage collector next runs
options.explanation: False. This Vec owns its buffer and normally releases it when dropped; it does not await a tracing collector. Intentional leaks and abort paths need not run Drop.

options.text: `let w = v;` copies the 24-byte header, not its heap buffer, and `v` can no longer be used
options.explanation: True. This is a move: the pointer, length and capacity are copied into `w`, ownership transfers, and the compiler rejects later uses of `v` so its heap buffer is never freed twice.

questions.workedExample:
Draw the layout:

```
 stack (v)        heap
 +-----------+    +---+---+---+
 | ptr  -----+--> | 1 | 2 | 3 |
 | len = 3   |    +---+---+---+
 | cap = 3   |     12 bytes
 +-----------+
  3 x 8 = 24 bytes
```

1. Three words on the stack: 24 bytes.
2. Three 4-byte integers on the heap: 12 bytes.
3. Freeing happens when the owner's scope ends, with no GC.
4. `let w = v;` copies the three words and marks `v` as moved. Only `w` will free its heap buffer.

The two sizes, as a calculation:

```formula
S_header = 3 × 8 B = 24 B
S_buffer = 3 × 4 B = 12 B
where
S_header: the size of the Vec value itself (pointer, length, capacity), in bytes (B)
S_buffer: the size of its heap buffer holding the elements, in bytes
3: three header fields in the first line; three elements in the second
8: the size of a pointer or usize on a 64-bit target, in bytes
4: the size of one i32 (a 32-bit integer), in bytes
B: bytes
In words: the Vec's header is three 8-byte words, 24 bytes, while the three 4-byte integers it owns take 12 bytes on the heap.
```

This describes the ownership/layout model; the compiler can eliminate physical copies or allocations when observable behavior is preserved.

lessons.title: Five manual-memory failure patterns
lessons.summary: Leaks retain allocations; use-after-free, double free, out-of-bounds writes and uninitialised reads violate separate rules
lessons.body:
Before choosing a tool or a repair, identify which allocation rule failed. These examples deliberately contain bugs; their invalid accesses have no guaranteed output.

## The five classic bugs

### 1. Memory leak

Memory that is never freed, typically because the last pointer to it was lost.

```c
void handle(void) {
    char *buf = malloc(4096);
    if (!buf) return;
    /* Fill buf before parsing. */
    /* Failure bypasses the release
     * below. */
    if (parse(buf) < 0)
        return;          /* leak: no free */
    free(buf);
}
```

An ordinary process exit reclaims its address space, so a small bounded leak in a short-lived tool may have limited impact. In an illustrative server, leaking 4,000 bytes per request at 1,000 requests/s accumulates 345.6 GB per day (decimal). The time and mode of failure depend on memory limits, allocation behavior and the environment; an OOM kill within hours is not guaranteed.

The daily figure is the leak rate multiplied by the number of seconds in a day:

```formula
R = 4,000 B/req × 1,000 req/s
R = 4,000,000 B/s
D = R × 86,400 s
D = 345,600,000,000 B = 345.6 GB
where
R: the leak rate: bytes lost per second
B: bytes
req: one request handled by the server
s: seconds
D: the memory leaked in one day, in bytes
86,400: the number of seconds in a day (24 × 60 × 60)
GB: gigabyte, 1,000,000,000 bytes (decimal)
In words: 4 kB lost on each of 1,000 requests a second is 4 MB a second, which over a day adds up to about 346 GB.
```

The model assumes a steady request rate and that nothing frees the leaked memory; real traffic varies through the day, so treat it as an order-of-magnitude warning, not a prediction.

### 2. Use-after-free

Reading or writing a block after it has been freed. The pointer still holds the old address (a **dangling pointer**), and the allocator may already have given that memory to someone else.

```c
struct user *u = find_user(id);
/* u becomes invalid for object access. */
free(u);
log_access(u->name);  /* use-after-free */
```

### 3. Double free

Calling `free` twice on the same block. This is undefined behavior. An allocator may detect and abort, or corruption and later exploitation may result; no specific allocator outcome is guaranteed.

### 4. Buffer overflow

Writing past the end (or before the start) of a block, trampling the allocator's metadata or a neighbouring object.

```c
char *s = malloc(strlen(src));  /* no +1 */
/* Copy includes the missing NUL byte. */
strcpy(s, src);   /* writes NUL past end */
```

### 5. Uninitialised read

Using `malloc`'d memory before writing it. Its contents are indeterminate; stale bytes can cause information disclosure, and reading an uninitialized typed value can invoke undefined behavior. Fresh pages may happen to be zero-filled, but malloc does not promise initialization.

| Bug | Symptom | Danger |
|---|---|---|
| Leak | memory grows | outage |
| Use-after-free | random corruption | exploit |
| Double free | allocator crash | exploit |
| Overflow | corruption | exploit |
| Uninit read | odd values | info leak |

## Key takeaways
- Leaks retain allocations; use-after-free, double free, out-of-bounds writes and uninitialised reads violate separate rules.
- A dangling pointer is not made safe by an allocator leaving familiar bytes behind.
- A steady leak-rate calculation is a sizing model, not a prediction of the exact time or mode of process failure.

## Further reading
- [Memory safety — Chromium security](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/memory-safety/)
- [AddressSanitizer — Clang documentation](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html)
- [Valgrind quick start guide](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/quick-start.html)
- [CWE-416: Use After Free — MITRE](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/416.html)
- [Resource acquisition is initialization — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_acquisition_is_initialization)
- [Region-based memory management — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Region-based_memory_management)
- [Primary verification source 1](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [Primary verification source 5](https://eel.is/c++draft/unique.ptr.single)

questions.prompt: A pointer still holds the address of a block that has been passed to `free`. What is that pointer called, and what is using it?

options.text: A dangling pointer; using it is a use-after-free
options.explanation: Correct. The pointer refers to memory the program no longer owns. Reading or writing through it is undefined behaviour and a common exploit primitive.

options.text: A null pointer; using it is a null dereference
options.explanation: free does not assign NULL into pointer variables. Their stored bits may remain, but pointers to the ended allocation become indeterminate under C lifetime rules; do not dereference them.

options.text: A wild pointer; using it is a memory leak
options.explanation: A leak is memory still allocated with no pointer to it, the opposite situation. Here the pointer survives but the memory has gone.

options.text: A smart pointer; using it is safe because the allocator tracks it
options.explanation: C's allocator does not track your pointers at all. Nothing stops you using a freed address.

questions.workedExample: After free, the allocation lifetime ends and aliases to it are dangling; reading or writing through them is undefined behavior. The stored bits are not automatically replaced with NULL, but the C pointer value becomes indeterminate under lifetime rules. Assigning p = NULL can prevent a second free through that variable because free(NULL) is allowed; dereferencing NULL remains undefined behavior and is not a guaranteed clean crash. Other aliases remain dangling.

questions.prompt: A small command-line tool runs for 200 ms, allocates a few megabytes and never calls `free`. A long-running server leaks 4,000 bytes on every request at 1,000 requests a second. Which statement is right?

options.text: Both are equally serious because every leak eventually crashes
options.explanation: A small bounded leak in a short-lived process differs from unbounded growth. It is not necessarily equally consequential.

options.text: Neither matters, because the OS frees leaked memory periodically
options.explanation: The OS does not identify unreachable malloc blocks and periodically free those allocations for a running C program. It can reclaim physical pages under virtual-memory policy; process exit releases the address space.

options.text: The server is fine because 4 KB is less than a page
options.explanation: Small leaks add up. Size per leak matters far less than the rate multiplied by uptime.

options.text: The short-lived allocation has limited retention cost; the server accumulates about 346 GB/day
options.explanation: Correct under the stated rate. Memory exhaustion risk grows, but failure timing and behavior depend on limits and allocation patterns.

questions.workedExample:
In the assumed hosted process, exit reclaims the address space, so the small short-lived allocation has limited retention cost. The server's daily leak is its leak rate times the seconds in a day:

```formula
R = 4,000 B/req × 1,000 req/s
R = 4,000,000 B/s
D = R × 86,400 s
D = 345,600,000,000 B
D = 345.6 GB
where
R: the leak rate, in bytes per second (B/s)
B: bytes
req: one request
s: seconds
D: the memory leaked per day, in bytes
86,400: seconds in a day (24 × 60 × 60)
GB: gigabyte, 1,000,000,000 bytes (decimal)
In words: 4,000 bytes on each of 1,000 requests a second is 4 MB a second, about 346 GB a day.
```
 Time and type of resource failure depend on limits and workload; there is no guaranteed OOM-kill schedule.

options.text: It always prints `ann`, because `free` does not erase memory
options.explanation: It might print `ann`, but nothing guarantees it. The freed slot may already have been reused by the next allocation.

options.text: The second `malloc` fails because the memory is still referenced by `u`
options.explanation: The allocator has no idea `u` still exists. Once freed, the block is fair game for any allocation.

options.text: It is undefined behaviour; with typical allocators `m` may reuse `u`'s slot, so `u->name` reads bytes that now belong to `m`
options.explanation: Correct. This is a use-after-free. Many allocators hand a just-freed block of the same size straight back, so `u` and `m` alias, and `u->name` is now whatever bytes `m` put there.

options.text: It prints an empty string because `free` zeroes the block
options.explanation: Standard `free` does not zero memory. Some debugging allocators poison freed memory, but that is not the C contract.

questions.workedExample:
1. `free(u)` returns the block to the allocator. `u` still holds its address.
2. Allocators keep per-size free lists. A request for the same size often gets the most recently freed block back.
3. So `m` may equal `u`. Writing `m->text` overwrites the bytes where `u->name` used to be.
4. `u->name` is now interpreted from those bytes: garbage, a crash, or attacker-chosen data.

This is the core of many real exploits: free an object, get attacker-controlled data allocated into the same slot, then use the dangling pointer. AddressSanitizer reports it as `heap-use-after-free`.

lessons.title: Memory safety and diagnostic tools
lessons.summary: Reusing a freed object's slot can turn a dangling function pointer into attacker-controlled execution, subject to allocator behaviour and defences
lessons.body:
Memory corruption can cross a security boundary rather than merely crash. Tools help find exercised failures, while language and library contracts determine which operations are valid.

## Why these are security holes

These bugs are not just crashes. Consider a use-after-free:

1. The program frees an object that contains a function pointer, but keeps a dangling pointer to it.
2. An attacker triggers an allocation of the same size with contents they control (say, a string from a network packet). The allocator reuses the freed slot.
3. The program calls through its dangling pointer, reading the attacker's bytes as a function address.

If the slot is reused as assumed and control-flow defenses do not stop the call through the corrupted pointer, this can enable arbitrary code execution. Overflows and double frees can be turned into similar primitives.

Chromium’s published analysis reported roughly 70% of its high-severity security bugs as memory-safety issues, with use-after-free a major category. Treat this as the historical dataset described by the source, not a measured current rate across all products. A separate universal Microsoft annual percentage is omitted here because this review has not established its applicable period and dataset. This is why governments and large companies now push new code towards **memory-safe languages**: Java, Go, Python, C#, Swift and Rust.

> [!note] What "memory safe" means
> A memory-safe language guarantees you cannot read or write memory you do not own: no dangling pointers, no out-of-bounds access, no double free. GC languages achieve it by never freeing reachable memory and bounds-checking arrays. Rust combines static ownership checks with runtime checks such as bounds checks and library synchronization; unsafe code and native interfaces remain obligations in all these systems.

## Finding the bugs

- **AddressSanitizer** (`-fsanitize=address` in Clang and GCC) instruments relevant memory accesses in compiled code; uninstrumented code and other coverage limitations remain. It reports heap-use-after-free, buffer overflows and double frees with stack traces, with a typical slowdown of about 2x, so you can run your test suite under it.
- **Valgrind Memcheck** runs an unmodified binary on a simulated CPU. No recompilation, but programs run roughly 20 to 30 times slower.
- **LeakSanitizer** and Valgrind's `--leak-check=yes` report blocks still allocated at exit with no pointer to them.
- **Fuzzers** (libFuzzer, AFL) combined with sanitizers find the inputs that trigger these bugs.

These find bugs in the code paths you exercise. They cannot prove their absence. Sound safe-language implementations instead enforce a class of validity rules for supported operations; unsafe code, native interfaces and implementation bugs remain obligations.

## Key takeaways
- Reusing a freed object's slot can turn a dangling function pointer into attacker-controlled execution, subject to allocator behaviour and defences.
- AddressSanitizer instruments compiled code; Memcheck can analyse a supported existing binary without rebuilding it.
- Passing sanitizer tests proves neither complete path coverage nor absence of all memory errors; quoted slowdown factors are documentation estimates.

## Further reading
- [Memory safety — Chromium security](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/memory-safety/)
- [AddressSanitizer — Clang documentation](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html)
- [Valgrind quick start guide](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/quick-start.html)
- [CWE-416: Use After Free — MITRE](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/416.html)
- [Resource acquisition is initialization — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_acquisition_is_initialization)
- [Region-based memory management — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Region-based_memory_management)
- [Primary verification source 1](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [Primary verification source 5](https://eel.is/c++draft/unique.ptr.single)

questions.prompt: An attacker can make a server free an object containing a function pointer while a dangling pointer to it survives, and can then send a packet whose payload is copied into a newly allocated block of the same size. Why is this so dangerous?

options.text: It only causes a crash, because freed memory is unmapped from the process
options.explanation: Small freed blocks stay mapped and are recycled by the allocator. They are not unmapped, so they can be reused with new contents.

options.text: It leaks the old object's memory, eventually exhausting the heap
options.explanation: The memory is reused, not leaked. The problem is aliasing, not growth.

options.text: It is harmless if the server uses `calloc`, which zeroes memory
options.explanation: `calloc` zeroes the new block at allocation, but the attacker then fills it with their payload. Zeroing does not stop the aliasing.

options.text: The new block can occupy the freed slot, so the next call through the dangling pointer jumps to an address the attacker chose
options.explanation: Correct. This is the classic use-after-free exploitation pattern: reclaim the slot with controlled bytes, then let the program use its stale pointer to call or write somewhere useful to the attacker.

questions.workedExample: If the allocator reuses the freed slot, attacker-controlled bytes can replace a stored callback address. A later call through the dangling pointer can then redirect control flow unless mitigations stop it. Neither slot reuse nor successful code execution is guaranteed by C. Chromium’s cited historical analysis covered 912 high/critical bugs since 2015: about 70% involved memory unsafety, and about half of those were use-after-free.

questions.prompt: You must choose a tool to find a suspected use-after-free in a third-party Linux binary for which you have no source code. Which is the better first choice?

options.text: Valgrind Memcheck, because it runs unmodified binaries on a simulated CPU
options.explanation: Correct for a supported Linux binary and platform. Memcheck instruments the machine code dynamically, tracking memory accesses and allocation state without rebuilding; the documentation quotes a typical slowdown of roughly 20–30 times.

options.text: AddressSanitizer, because it is faster
options.explanation: ASan normally needs compiler instrumentation and its runtime for general access checking. Runtime interposition can detect some external-library errors, but it does not comprehensively instrument an arbitrary existing binary; Memcheck fits this constraint better.

options.text: LeakSanitizer, because use-after-free is a kind of leak
options.explanation: A use-after-free accesses storage after deallocation; a leak leaves an allocation unreclaimed. Standalone LeakSanitizer can work by linking its runtime without compiler access instrumentation, but it is a leak detector, not this use-after-free tool.

options.text: Neither; use-after-free can only be found by code review
options.explanation: Dynamic tools find these routinely, with stack traces of the allocation, the free and the bad access.

questions.workedExample:
1. Constraint: no source, so you cannot recompile with `-fsanitize=address`.
2. Valgrind translates the binary's machine code as it runs, adding checks to each memory access.
3. Trade-off table:

| | ASan | Memcheck |
|---|---|---|
| Rebuild | yes | no |
| Slowdown | ~2x | ~20-30x |

lessons.title: Cleanup paths, arenas and RAII
lessons.summary: A cleanup label can release every resource acquired before any failure, and free(NULL) needs no special case

options.text: Because `goto` automatically frees memory allocated before it
options.explanation: `goto` is just a jump. It frees nothing by itself.

options.text: Because `buf` starts as `NULL`, every path reaches `out:`, and `free(NULL)` is defined to do nothing
options.explanation: Correct. Initialising to `NULL` means the early `goto` on a failed `fopen` reaches `free(buf)` with `buf == NULL`, which the C standard defines as a no-op.

options.text: Because the compiler inserts `free` calls at every `return`
options.explanation: Ordinary C has no language rule that inserts a matching free for every allocation on return. This function explicitly calls free in its cleanup block; C++ resource-owning RAII objects provide a different mechanism.

options.text: It doesn't: when `fopen` fails, `free(buf)` is undefined behaviour
options.explanation: It would be if `buf` were uninitialised. Because it is set to `NULL` first, `free(NULL)` is well defined and harmless.

questions.workedExample:
Trace each path:

1. `fopen` fails: `buf` is `NULL`, jump to `out`. `free(NULL)` does nothing; `fp` is `NULL`, so no `fclose`. Return -1.
2. `malloc` fails: `fp` is open, `buf` is `NULL`. `free(NULL)` is a no-op; `fclose(fp)` runs. Return -1.
3. Success: both acquired, both released. Return 0.

Every path runs one cleanup block, so nothing leaks and nothing is freed twice. This single-exit pattern is used throughout the Linux kernel.

questions.prompt: A C++ function creates `auto p = std::make_unique<Widget>();` and then calls a function that throws an exception. What happens to the `Widget`? Assume a handler outside the function catches the exception, with ordinary stack unwinding.

options.text: It is freed when the exception unwinds the stack, because `p`'s destructor runs
options.explanation: Correct. Stack unwinding runs the destructors of every local object in the abandoned frames. `~unique_ptr` deletes the `Widget`. This is RAII.

options.text: It leaks, because the `delete` line after the call is skipped
options.explanation: That is what happens with a raw `new` and a manual `delete`. `unique_ptr` exists precisely to avoid it.

options.text: It is freed later by the C++ garbage collector
options.explanation: Standard C++ has no garbage collector. Memory is released deterministically by destructors.

options.text: The program terminates immediately, so it doesn't matter
options.explanation: An exception that is caught higher up does not terminate the program, and the destructors run during unwinding.

questions.workedExample:
1. RAII ties a resource to an object's lifetime.
2. `p` is a local object; its destructor runs whenever its scope ends, by normal return **or** by an exception.
3. During unwinding, C++ calls `~unique_ptr()`, which calls `delete` on the `Widget`.

Compare the raw version:

```cpp
Widget *w = new Widget;
mayThrow();     // throws
delete w;       // never reached: leak
```

The same idea frees locks (`std::lock_guard`), files and sockets.

questions.prompt: A compiler allocates millions of small AST nodes during one compilation pass and frees them all at the end. Which strategy is most appropriate, and why?

options.text: `malloc` and `free` each node individually, so memory is returned as early as possible

options.text: An arena: bump-allocate nodes from large blocks and free the whole arena when the pass ends
options.explanation: Correct. Allocation is a pointer bump, there are no individual frees to get wrong, and the whole region goes in one call. This fits objects that share one lifetime.

options.text: Reference count each node so they free themselves
options.explanation: Strong-owner creation and release can require count updates, and intact strong cycles need another mechanism. Borrowing/moves can avoid some updates; an arena matches this shared-lifetime task without per-node ownership counts.

options.text: Put the nodes on the stack, since the pass is a single function call
options.explanation: Millions of nodes would overflow a stack of a few megabytes, and the pass is many nested calls, not one frame.

questions.workedExample:
1. Note the lifetime pattern: every node is born during the pass and dies at its end.
2. When objects share a lifetime, tracking them individually is wasted effort.
3. An arena grabs big chunks and hands out memory by bumping a pointer:

```
[node|node|node|node|  free...  ]
                    ^ next
```

4. At the end, free the chunks. No per-node bookkeeping, no dangling pointers within the pass.

Clang, Rust's compiler, game engines (per-frame arenas) and nginx (per-request pools) all use this.

lessons.title: Reachability leaks and resource cleanup
lessons.summary: Reachable but obsolete cache entries cannot be identified as unnecessary by ordinary reachability collection
lessons.body:
A collector answers whether an object is reachable, not whether retaining it still serves the application. Memory retention and resource release therefore remain design responsibilities even in a managed language.

## Garbage collection is not a cure for leaks

GC languages free memory only when it becomes **unreachable**. If your program keeps a reference, the memory stays, even if you will never use it again. These are logical leaks:

```python
_cache = {}

def get_report(user_id, day):
    key = (user_id, day)
    # Each distinct key can retain a report.
    if key not in _cache:
        _cache[key] = build_report(
            user_id, day)
    return _cache[key]   # grows forever
```

Common culprits in Python, Java and Go: unbounded caches and maps, listeners or callbacks that are registered and never removed, static collections, and (in Go) goroutines blocked forever on a channel, which pin everything they reference.

GC also does not manage **other resources**. Files, sockets and locks must still be released deterministically:

| Language | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Python | `with open(...) as f:` |
| Java | try-with-resources |
| Go | `defer f.Close()` |
| C++ / Rust | destructor / `Drop` |

## Bound the retention policy

For the report cache, specify an eviction or expiry rule as well as a lookup rule. A test can request many distinct user-and-day pairs and inspect whether obsolete entries leave the cache. A bounded cache may intentionally retain useful reports; indefinite retention without a useful policy is the logical leak.

A blocked goroutine can also retain values needed by its suspended computation. Arrange cancellation or a channel protocol that lets it return, rather than assuming a collector will terminate the goroutine. Exact retained bytes depend on compiler liveness and runtime representation.

Files and sockets use operating-system resources in addition to any small wrapper object. Closing them promptly avoids exhausting descriptors even when plenty of heap remains. Use the language's explicit cleanup construct and handle close errors where they matter, rather than relying on an unspecified finalizer schedule.

## Key takeaways
- Reachable but obsolete cache entries cannot be identified as unnecessary by ordinary reachability collection.
- Cancellation, listener removal and bounded cache policies control logical retention.
- Use with, try-with-resources, defer or documented destructor behaviour to release non-memory resources promptly.

## Further reading
- [Memory safety — Chromium security](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/memory-safety/)
- [AddressSanitizer — Clang documentation](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html)
- [Valgrind quick start guide](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/quick-start.html)
- [CWE-416: Use After Free — MITRE](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/416.html)
- [Resource acquisition is initialization — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_acquisition_is_initialization)
- [Region-based memory management — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Region-based_memory_management)
- [Primary verification source 1](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [Primary verification source 5](https://eel.is/c++draft/unique.ptr.single)

options.text: A module-level dict used as a cache that is never evicted
options.explanation: Correct. Every entry stays reachable from a global, so the GC can never free it, even if it will never be read again.

options.text: An event listener registered on a long-lived object and never removed
options.explanation: Correct. The long-lived object holds a reference to the listener, and through it everything the listener captures.

options.text: A goroutine blocked forever receiving on a channel nobody sends to
options.explanation: A permanently blocked goroutine is not collected merely because it is blocked. Values still needed by its suspended computation can remain reachable; compiler liveness determines what is actually retained.

options.text: A local list created inside a function and not returned
options.explanation: Under the stated no-escape assumption, the list can become unreachable and eligible for reclamation. The language/runtime does not promise a collection immediately on return.

options.text: Two objects that refer only to each other, in Java
options.explanation: Java's tracing collector frees anything unreachable from the roots, cycles included. (CPython's reference counting alone could not, but its cycle collector does.)

questions.workedExample:
A GC frees memory that is **unreachable**. A leak in a GC language is memory that is still **reachable** but will never be used.

1. Global cache: reachable from a module global. Leak.
2. Listener: reachable from the long-lived subject's listener list. Leak.
3. Blocked goroutine: goroutines are roots; its stack keeps its data alive. Leak.
4. Local list: no references after return. Collected.
5. Cycle in Java: unreachable from roots, so a tracing GC collects it.

The fix is the same in each leaky case: bound the structure (an LRU cache), unregister, or give the goroutine a way to exit (a `context` or a closed channel).

lessons.title: Strong counts and prompt release
lessons.summary: The basic eager-counting model tracks strong owners and reclaims an acyclic, non-resurrecting value when its last owner releases it
lessons.body:
The simplest automatic answer to "when can this object be freed?" is: **when nobody refers to it any more**. Keep a counter in every object of how many references point at it. When the counter drops to zero, free the object.

That is **reference counting**. It runs inside CPython, Swift and Objective-C (as ARC), PHP, Perl, C++'s `std::shared_ptr` and Rust's `Rc` and `Arc`. It is easy to understand, it frees memory promptly, and it has one famous blind spot: **cycles**.

## The mechanism

In the basic model each managed allocation has a strong-reference count (possibly in a separate control block). The runtime (or the compiler) adjusts it whenever a reference is created or destroyed:

- A reference is **created** (assignment, passing an argument, putting it in a list): increment.
- A reference is **destroyed** (a variable is reassigned or goes out of scope, an item is removed): decrement.
- The count reaches **zero**: free the object, and decrement everything **it** refers to.

```
 a = Obj()        Obj  rc=1  <- a
 b = a            Obj  rc=2  <- a, b
 del a            Obj  rc=1  <- b
 b = None         Obj  rc=0  -> freed
```

That last rule can create a **cascading release**. In an exclusively owned acyclic linked list, releasing the head can make each successor lose its last owner. Implementations can use worklists or other techniques rather than literal native-stack recursion.

In the trace above, each `rc=` value is the object's reference count. Each update is a single addition or subtraction:

```formula
rc' = rc + 1
rc' = rc − 1
where
rc: the object's reference count before the change: how many strong references currently point at it
rc': the count after the change; the first line applies when a reference is created, the second when one is destroyed
In words: creating a reference adds one, destroying one subtracts one, and the object is freed at the moment the count reaches 0.
```

Following the trace: `Obj()` starts at 1, `b = a` makes it 1 + 1 = 2, `del a` makes it 2 − 1 = 1, and `b = None` makes it 1 − 1 = 0, so the object is freed. The model assumes every reference is counted; weak references (below) deliberately are not.

## Watching it in CPython

In ordinary GIL-enabled CPython, object headers include reference-count metadata. This simple non-resurrecting example illustrates prompt finalization; free-threaded/deferred counting, cycles and finalizers can alter timing:

```python
class Noisy:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def __del__(self):
        print("freed", self.name)

a = Noisy("a")
b = a
# b still holds this object alive.
del a
print("after del a")
# Last owner leaves in this CPython example.
del b
print("after del b")
```

Output:

```
after del a
freed a
after del b
```

`del a` only drops the count from 2 to 1, because `b` still refers to the object. `del b` drops it to 0, so the object is freed immediately, before the next line runs.

> [!note] Immortal objects
> Since Python 3.12, objects such as `None`, `True` and small integers are **immortal objects** (PEP 683): reference-count operations treat them specially and ordinary decrements do not deallocate them. The large reported count is not a reliable count of live references or a stable universal constant.

## Why people like it

1. **Promptness.** Acyclic, non-resurrecting objects can be reclaimed promptly when their last strong owner releases them; allocator retention can still keep process memory high.
2. **Deterministic destruction.** Simple eager counting has predictable release points. For files use with/open, RAII or explicit close; temporary-object destruction is not a portable resource-management guarantee, and cycles or deferred counting can delay it.
3. **Incremental by nature.** The work is spread across the program, without requiring a separate whole-heap collection in the basic acyclic model; cascading release can still take substantial time.
4. **Locality.** Basic count updates touch ownership metadata for the affected values rather than scanning an entire heap; releasing a final owner can touch further objects.

## Key takeaways
- The basic eager-counting model tracks strong owners and reclaims an acyclic, non-resurrecting value when its last owner releases it.
- Deleting one Python name does not destroy an object retained by another name.
- Cycles, deferred counting, immortal objects and finalizers qualify any claim of universally immediate destruction.

## Further reading

- [Python gc module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/gc.html)
- [Python weakref module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/weakref.html)
- [Automatic Reference Counting — The Swift Programming Language](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/automaticreferencecounting/)
- [Rc and reference cycles — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-06-reference-cycles.html)

- [Primary verification source 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift-book/main/TSPL.docc/LanguageGuide/AutomaticReferenceCounting.md)

print("one")

lessons.title: The costs of keeping counts
lessons.summary: Count traffic, metadata, synchronisation and cascading release can each cost time or space
lessons.body:
Reference counts replace a whole-heap tracing decision with ownership bookkeeping along execution paths. That work can be cheap in one setting and expensive in another; measure the actual implementation and sharing pattern.

## What it costs

Reference counting is not free. Creating or releasing a strong ownership reference can require count traffic. Borrowed references, moves, immortal objects and optimization can avoid updates.

- **Count updates everywhere.** Passing, storing or returning strong references can touch counts, depending on borrowing conventions and optimization. In CPython this is a measurable share of interpreter time.
- **Atomic operations under threads.** Concurrent strong-count updates require synchronization, often atomic operations whose cost depends on hardware, contention and memory ordering. C++ `shared_ptr` and Rust `Arc` pay this; Rust's `Rc` does not, and the compiler refuses to let an `Rc` cross threads. CPython's GIL let it use plain increments; the free-threaded build (PEP 703) uses **biased reference counting**, where the owning thread updates a fast local count and other threads use an atomic shared one.
- **Space.** Counts and related metadata use storage; their size varies by implementation (in `shared_ptr`, usually a separate control block).
- **Cascading frees.** In the simple eager model, dropping the last owner of an exclusively owned acyclic 10-million-node tree can require releasing all 10 million nodes before returning. Shared owners, cycles or deferred destruction change that work; eager counting alone gives no short-pause bound.
- **Copy-on-write damage.** Some operations acquiring references write counts, which can dirty shared pages after fork. The cycle collector also changes bookkeeping. gc.freeze() (Python 3.7) avoids collector traversal of frozen objects; it does not suppress their ordinary reference-count updates.

> [!tip] Avoiding count traffic
> C++ code passes `const std::shared_ptr<T>&`, or a plain `T&`, when the callee does not need to keep the object. Swift's optimiser removes retain/release pairs it can prove redundant. Rust makes clones of `Rc` explicit with `Rc::clone(&x)` so you can see each one.

## Choosing the ownership handle

Use Rc when shared ownership stays within a thread; Arc synchronises its ownership counts for use across threads when the contained type satisfies the required thread-safety traits. Arc does not by itself synchronise accesses to the contained data. In C++, separate shared_ptr handles sharing a control block can be updated concurrently; simultaneous unsynchronised writes to the same handle are a different issue.

After fork, reference-count writes and collector bookkeeping can dirty otherwise shared private pages. The resulting copies depend on the pages actually touched, not simply on the number of workers. CPython's freeze operation avoids later cycle-collector bookkeeping on frozen objects; ordinary counting writes can still occur. Keeping a dataset semantically read-only does not guarantee that its runtime metadata is never written.

## Key takeaways
- Count traffic, metadata, synchronisation and cascading release can each cost time or space.
- Borrowing, moving and compiler optimisation can avoid some reference-count updates.
- Rc and Arc express different thread-sharing contracts; neither a logical read-only dataset nor gc.freeze promises zero copy-on-write page copying.

## Further reading
- [Reference counting — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_counting)
- [Python gc module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/gc.html)
- [Python weakref module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/weakref.html)
- [Automatic Reference Counting — The Swift Programming Language](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/automaticreferencecounting/)
- [Rc and reference cycles — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-06-reference-cycles.html)
- [PEP 683: Immortal objects](https://peps.python.org/pep-0683/)
- [Primary verification source 2](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/refcounting.html)
- [Primary verification source 3](https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/)
- [Primary verification source 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift-book/main/TSPL.docc/LanguageGuide/AutomaticReferenceCounting.md)
- [Primary verification source 5](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html)

lessons.title: Cycles and weak ownership edges
lessons.summary: An intact unreachable strong cycle keeps its own counts above zero under pure reference counting
lessons.body:
A strong-reference count records incoming owners, not reachability from the running program. A group can therefore own itself after every outside reference disappears.

## The cycle problem

In the diagram, A and B name the two objects, x and y are outside references, and rc labels each object's strong-reference count. It is a toy ownership graph with no additional references.

Two objects that refer to each other each hold a count of at least 1, forever, even when nothing else can reach them.

```
 before:  x --> [A rc=2] --> [B rc=2] <-- y
                   ^------------'

 after del x, y:
          [A rc=1] --> [B rc=1]
             ^------------'
          unreachable, never freed
```

Cycles are everywhere in real programs: a parent node and its children with `parent` pointers, a doubly linked list, an object that adds itself as a callback, an exception that holds a traceback that holds the frame that holds the exception.

Pure counting cannot reclaim an unreachable strong-reference cycle that remains intact. Weak edges, explicit link removal or a design that forbids strong cycles can avoid that situation. There are two fixes: make some references not count (weak references), or add a separate collector that finds cycles.

## Fix 1: weak references

A **weak reference** points at an object without contributing to its count. When the object is freed, the weak reference becomes empty instead of dangling.

The rule of thumb: **owners hold strong references, back-pointers are weak.** A parent owns its children; a child's pointer to its parent is weak.

| Language | Strong | Weak |
|---|---|---|
| Python | normal ref | `weakref.ref` |
| Swift | default strong | weak (nil on release); unowned has a different lifetime contract |
| C++ | `shared_ptr` | `weak_ptr` |
| Rust | `Rc` / `Arc` | `Weak` |

```python
import weakref

class Node:
    def __init__(self, parent=None):
        self.children = []
        # Back-pointer does not own the
        # parent.
        self._parent = (weakref.ref(parent)
                        if parent else None)

    @property
    def parent(self):
        ref = self._parent
        # A collected target resolves to
        # None.
        return ref() if ref else None
```

Calling the weak reference returns the object, or `None` if it has been freed. C++'s `weak_ptr::lock()` and Rust's `Weak::upgrade()` work the same way: they give you a temporary strong reference or nothing.

Swift adds `unowned`, a reference that does not keep its target strongly alive. You promise its target remains alive whenever it is accessed. Ordinary checked `unowned` traps on access after deallocation; `unowned(unsafe)` omits that protection. Swift closures are the classic cycle: a view controller stores a closure that captures `self` strongly. The fix is a capture list, `{ [weak self] in ... }`.

Weak references only help where you can see the cycle coming. Ordinary Swift/Objective-C ARC and C++ `shared_ptr` have no general tracing cycle collector. Explicitly clearing links can also break a cycle; a retained cycle otherwise leaks. Xcode provides a memory graph debugger to investigate such ownership.

## Key takeaways
- An intact unreachable strong cycle keeps its own counts above zero under pure reference counting.
- Choose weak back-pointers where the domain's ownership relation permits them; acquiring a weak target can fail.
- Swift checked unowned references carry a lifetime obligation and trap after target deallocation; they are not interchangeable with optional weak references.

## Further reading

3. Ownership flows downward, so make the upward pointer weak.
4. Dropping the root: the root's count falls to 0 and it is freed; it decrements each child to 0; they free their children, and so on.

Python `weakref.ref`, Swift `weak`, C++ `weak_ptr` and Rust `Weak` all express this.

Dropping the root only destroys children that have no other strong owners. A child retained elsewhere can survive with an empty weak parent reference.

lessons.title: Finding unreachable counted cycles
lessons.summary: Subtract candidate-internal edges from scratch counts, preserve external roots and everything they reach, then reclaim the remaining unreachable group
lessons.body:
CPython supplements strong-reference counting with a cycle collector. Its trial counts distinguish references coming from within a candidate group from references coming from the rest of the program.

## Fix 2: a cycle collector

CPython takes the belt-and-braces route: reference counting for the common case, plus a **cycle collector** in the `gc` module for the rest.

It only needs to consider **container objects** (lists, dicts, class instances), because ordinary built-in int and str instances do not contain references participating in cycles; subclasses and extension types can have different layouts. The algorithm is neat:

1. For each container being examined, copy its reference count into a scratch field.
2. For every reference *between* those containers, subtract one from the target's scratch count.
3. Anything left with a scratch count above zero is referenced from **outside** the group, so it is alive. Everything reachable from it is alive too.
4. Whatever remains is referenced only from inside the group: unreachable cycles. Free it.

Steps 1 and 2 compute, for each container, how many of its references come from outside the group:

```formula
g_X = rc_X − i_X
where
g_X: the scratch count for container X (CPython's source calls this field gc_refs)
rc_X: X's ordinary reference count
i_X: the number of references to X that come from other containers in the group being examined
In words: take an object's count and subtract the references the group itself holds; what is left are references from outside, such as local variables.
```

In the two-node example below, after `del x, y` each node has a reference count of 1 and one reference from inside the group (the other node points at it), so its scratch count is 1 − 1 = 0: nothing outside holds them, and they are freed. An object with a scratch count above zero is alive, and step 3 keeps everything reachable from it alive too, even objects whose own scratch count is 0.

```python
import gc
gc.disable()  # explicit collect still works

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.other = name, None
    def __del__(self):
        print("freed", self.name)

x, y = Node("x"), Node("y")
# Internal strong edges keep counts nonzero.
x.other, y.other = y, x
del x, y
print("after del")
# Explicitly find the unreachable cycle.
gc.collect()
print("collected")
gc.enable()
```

Output (the two "freed" lines may come in either order):

```
after del
freed x
freed y
collected
```

After `del x, y`, each node still has a count of 1 from the other, so nothing is freed. `gc.collect()` subtracts the internal references, finds both at zero, and frees them. Since Python 3.4 (PEP 442), a Python-level __del__ no longer by itself prevents collection of an unreachable cycle. Finalizers can still resurrect objects, and some extension types have different finalization constraints; gc.garbage is not universally empty.

The collector is a **generational collector**: new containers are examined often, survivors less often, to exploit workload-dependent short object lifetimes. Scheduling depends on version/build: net allocation counts matter, and free-threaded CPython also considers process-memory growth. The thresholds are tunable with `gc.set_threshold()`.

> [!warning] Disabling the cycle collector
> gc.disable() disables automatic cyclic collection. Reference counting still operates and explicit gc.collect() still works; unreachable intact strong cycles can accumulate until explicitly collected or broken. Some services do this deliberately for predictable latency and then must avoid creating cycles.

## Where reference counting sits

| | Ref counting | Tracing GC |
|---|---|---|
| When freed | last strong release in the basic acyclic model | during collection |
| Cycles | need extra help | traced normally |
| Cost paid on | strong-reference updates and cascading release | collection and barriers |
| Destruction | prompt in basic model | runtime-specific timing |

Many systems blend the two. CPython is reference counting plus a tracing cycle collector. Research collectors use **deferred reference counting**, which skips count updates for stack variables and corrects the counts periodically, to get most of the promptness with much less overhead.

## Key takeaways
- Subtract candidate-internal edges from scratch counts, preserve external roots and everything they reach, then reclaim the remaining unreachable group.
- gc.disable stops automatic cyclic collection, while reference counting and explicit gc.collect continue to operate.
- CPython collection schedules depend on version and build; finalization and resurrection complicate the simple trial-count model.
